title: Noguchi Hideyo and His Mother's Letter
text:
Noguchi Hideyo was born in 1876 into a poor farming family in Inawashiro, in northern Japan. When he was a baby, he fell into the open hearth while his mother, Shika, was working outside, and his left hand was badly burned, the fingers fused together. Shika blamed herself all her life. As a teenager he had an operation that partly restored the use of his hand, and the experience made him decide to become a doctor.

He qualified in medicine and in 1900 went to the United States. At the Rockefeller Institute in New York he became famous for his research, especially on syphilis, and was nominated several times for the Nobel Prize. He did not come home.

Shika had never been taught to read or write, but she taught herself as an adult. In 1912 she wrote to her son a letter in a clumsy hand, with many mistakes, begging him to come back. She wrote that she was waiting and that she wanted to see him, and asked him to come home soon, again and again. The letter is preserved and displayed at the Noguchi Hideyo Memorial Museum.

In 1915 Noguchi returned to Japan for the only time, and spent time travelling with his mother. She died in 1918. He died ten years later in Accra, in Africa, of yellow fever, the disease he had gone there to study.
lesson: Success far from home can make us forget those waiting for us. A visit we keep postponing may be the one that matters most.
location: Inawashiro, Fukushima, Japan, and New York, USA
source: Letter of Noguchi Shika (1912), Noguchi Hideyo Memorial Museum; Isabel R. Plesset, Noguchi and His Patrons (1980)
caveat: Some of Noguchi's scientific claims were later shown to be wrong.
